rule: A shareholder of an S corporation includes in gross income the shareholder’s pro rata share of the corporation’s income and separately stated items for the corporation’s taxable year, while distributions are generally not included in gross income except to the extent they exceed stock basis.
explanation: An S corporation shareholder reports the shareholder’s pro rata share of the corporation’s income, whether or not distributions are made. Carson’s 40% share of $400,000 is $160,000; the $28,000 cash distribution is not added because an S corporation distribution is generally tax-free to the extent of stock basis.

quotes.quote: In determining the tax under this chapter of a shareholder for the shareholder’s taxable year in which the taxable year of the S corporation ends (or for the final taxable year of a shareholder who dies, or of a trust or estate which terminates, before the end of the corporation’s taxable year), there shall be taken into account the shareholder’s pro rata share of the corporation’s—

In any case where it is necessary to determine the gross income of a shareholder for purposes of this title, such gross income shall include the shareholder’s pro rata share of the gross income of the corporation.
The distribution shall not be included in gross income to the extent that it does not exceed the adjusted basis of the stock.

gate_log.why: The cited statutes support including Carson's 40% pro rata share of $400,000 ($160,000) and excluding the $28,000 distribution to the extent of stock basis, so the chosen answer is consistent with the sources. The researcher should confirm the basis ordering under §1367(a), showing that the current-year $160,000 income share increases basis before the $28,000 distribution, so the distribution is fully sheltered.

rule: Under the last-in, first-out method, goods remaining in ending inventory are treated as consisting first of beginning inventory and then of current-year acquisitions, so cost of goods sold is assigned from the most recently acquired units first.
explanation: Under LIFO, the 50,000 units sold are assigned first to the most recent purchases: 40,000 units at $17 plus 10,000 units at $15. Cost of goods sold is therefore $680,000 + $150,000 = $830,000.
